segs.text: Module seven A, objective three. Factors that can influence bioavailability. F is the fraction of a dose that reaches the systemic circulation, with no units, and it is one for an I V dose. An oral dose has to leave the product, dissolve, survive the stomach and gut, cross the gut wall and pass the liver before it reaches the circulation, and F counts only what arrives. These factors change how much arrives, so they can lower F or raise it. Her list has nine entries: in the product, on the way into the circulation, and in the patient.

card.m: F = fraction reaching the systemic circulation; F<sub>IV</sub> = 1
product → dissolved → gut → gut wall → liver → circulation: F counts what arrives
factors change how much arrives: F can go down or up
the product; on the way in; the patient

segs.text: First, the product. The physicochemical properties of the drug and the formulation, such as solubility, dissolution rate and particle size, decide how much drug dissolves and can be absorbed, and a better formulation can raise F. A drug that breaks down in acid is partly destroyed in the low p H of the stomach, so stability and p H effects lower its oral F. A prodrug is usually an inactive form that the body converts to the active drug, used to improve solubility or stability, or to raise the active drug's availability by decreasing first pass metabolism. She singled out the physical and chemical properties of the drug, what p H does to it in the body, first pass metabolism, and stability.

card.m: properties, formulation: how much dissolves and can be absorbed
acid-labile drug: degraded in the stomach → F lower
prodrug: usually inactive → active; for solubility, stability, or less first-pass
most often: properties, pH, first-pass, stability

segs.text: Next, the way in. Pre systemic metabolism is any metabolism before the drug reaches the systemic circulation, and first pass metabolism is the liver acting on an oral dose on its way from the gut. Absorbed is not the same as available: the textbook's propranolol is almost completely absorbed, but first pass metabolism leaves only about a quarter of it to reach the circulation. Food can lower F, raise it, or leave it unchanged, and a second drug that inhibits the metabolizing enzymes raises F while one that induces them lowers it. Efflux transporters are membrane proteins that pump absorbed drug back out of the cell, so they reduce how much gets through.

card.m: pre-systemic: any loss before the systemic circulation
first-pass: the liver, on an oral dose
propranolol: almost all absorbed, about 25% reaches the circulation
food: lower, higher or no change
enzyme inhibitor → F higher; inducer → F lower
efflux transporters: pump drug back out → less gets through

segs.text: Last, the patient: age and disease state. She said, Yeah, because our bodies change as we age, and yes, everything slows down. The textbook says bioavailability can change with age and with disease state, so these patient factors can raise F or lower it. Her summary names the two causes of low bioavailability she stresses, formulation factors and the first pass effect, and ties bioavailability to the drug's safety and efficacy.

card.m: age, disease state: can raise or lower F (textbook)
low F: formulation factors, first-pass effect
→ safety and efficacy

segs.text: Her first practice problem in objective two gave a tablet an F of zero point five five. So from a one thousand milligram tablet about five hundred fifty milligrams reaches the circulation, while one thousand milligrams given I V is all available. The oral problems earlier in the course had F values of about zero point seven to zero point nine. She said, we're losing almost half the drug giving it orally, right? A low F raises the question of whether oral is the best route, and it raises the oral dose needed to match an I V dose, because that dose must make up for what is lost.

card.m: F = 0.55 (objective two)
IV: F = 1 → all 1000 mg
earlier oral problems: F about 0.7 to 0.9
low F → larger oral dose to match IV (objective four)

segs.text: Her items keep F apart from what happens after the drug arrives. A low F is keyed to first pass metabolism and formulation factors, not to the half life, the volume of distribution, or a low clearance. F is the fraction that gets into the circulation, while clearance and half life act after it gets there, so they change the area under the curve, not F. Write F as zero point five five or fifty five percent. She said, just a little reminder, there should be no leading decimals, OK?

card.m: low F: first-pass, formulation. not t<sub>½</sub>, V<sub>D</sub> or clearance
F: how much enters. Cl, t<sub>½</sub>: act after → change AUC, not F
write 0.55 or 55%
